subject: Computer Networking
title: WebAssembly (Wasm)
description: A fast breakdown of WebAssembly (Wasm) for builders.

hook.text: JavaScript is fast. But for Photoshop in a browser, you need faster. WebAssembly runs at near-native speed.

buildup.text: Wasm is a binary format. Browsers execute it alongside JavaScript. C, C++, and Rust compile to Wasm.

discovery.text: Figma, Google Earth, and AutoCAD run in the browser via Wasm. Desktop-class apps, no install needed.

twist.text: Wasm doesn't replace JavaScript. They work together. JS handles the UI. Wasm handles heavy computation.

climax.text: WASI extends Wasm beyond browsers. Run Wasm on servers, edge, and IoT. A universal runtime is emerging.

punchline.text: Wasm brings native performance to the web. The browser is the new OS.

quiz.question: What languages can compile to WebAssembly?
options: C, C++, and Rust among others

details.summary: WebAssembly is a low-level binary format that runs in browsers at near-native speed alongside JavaScript.
details.whyItMatters: WebAssembly makes the browser a platform for applications that previously required native installation. It brings compiled-language performance to the web without sacrificing security.
takeaways: Wasm runs compiled code at near-native speed in browsers
C, C++, Rust, and other languages compile to WebAssembly
Sandboxed execution ensures security despite native-level speed

faq.question: Does WebAssembly replace JavaScript?
faq.answer: No. WebAssembly and JavaScript are complementary. JavaScript handles DOM manipulation, event handling, and orchestration. WebAssembly handles compute-intensive tasks like image processing, physics simulation, and cryptography.

faq.question: What applications use WebAssembly?
faq.answer: Figma runs its design tool in Wasm for performance. AutoCAD ported its desktop application to the web via Wasm. Google Earth uses it. Game engines like Unity export to Wasm. Video codecs, database engines, and AI inference also benefit from Wasm's near-native execution speed.
